Standing supervision of the AI agents that do work in My/Knowledge/Garden/logseq-encode-garden. One chief-of-staff agent holds this graph's docket from a tmux session of its own, starts subagents for named work items, and reports outcomes, so names the work and reads results instead of driving each session. Its subagents and worktrees run in the harness's own subagents or in tmux; herdr is used only when asks for it.

A hayward kept the hedges and fences of the common fields, and kept the livestock out of the growing crop. The work here is the same shape: deciding what may be written into a public garden, keeping another repository's private context from crossing into it, and keeping links pointing at pages that exist.

The name belongs to the seat rather than to whichever session is sitting in it. A session ends, a model changes, an agent renames itself; the seat and its record carry on, and whoever takes it next inherits both. encode-garden-chief-of-staff describes a function and changes with the workspace label — Hayward does not.

The register is the one the other seats use, from Person/Steve Yegge/Agent: a reeve ran one estate, a seneschal ran the household above them, a hayward held the boundary. No agent on that roster carries this name.

Chiefs are conventionally named <workspace>-chief-of-staff, and the name is a hint rather than a mechanism. It is not how one is found. An agent can rename itself out of the convention and go on supervising, a chief with no pane carries no multiplexer name at all, and a name can be reassigned to a different session while staying valid — so matching on the suffix has no case left where it is sufficient. One filter run against the live set returned two of the chiefs that were working at that moment.

Find them by enumerating the registry by reference and taking each agent's role from its own report, or from the declaration kept in the repository it supervises. A repository saying who supervises it is a local declaration; it is not a cross-repository roster anyone has to maintain.

The name is not how one is reached either. Sending to a bare name reaches whichever session currently answers to it, which after a rename or reassignment is not the one meant. Address by name together with the listing's own reference, read fresh at the moment of sending rather than from memory. Absence from any listing means unknown, never that no chief is there.
Chiefs over other repos work from the declaration kept in their own repo.

The role's general shape travels with the agent from repo to repo. What a repo declares for itself is its docket, what counts as done, which subagents it starts, who commits, and which calls a chief settles alone. Those are the sections below.

This graph holds one such declaration. The other chiefs' declarations sit in their own repos, where this graph cannot read them, so the role lives here as a single page rather than as a type under Logseq/Entity with a definition page and instances. An agent arriving cold reaches it by the path My/AI/Agent/Chief of Staff and by the Chief of Staff title, which makes a rename here a decision for .
The page sits beside My/AI/Agent/Ask My Agent Anything About Me under My/AI/Agent/, which holds what this repo declares to an agent working in it.
Frontmatter is a [[Diataxis/How To]] tag, a see-also:: line reaching the garden page, herdr, and Logseq/Journal, and a github-link:: to the file on GitHub.
The daily record is nested underneath at My/AI/Agent/Chief of Staff/Log/YY/MM/DD Ddd, following Logseq/Best Practice/Utilize Date Namespacing Under Entity Name.
Standing upkeep of the graph: today's journal current, pages filed where the graph's conventions put them, links resolving, edits committed, and the workspace left in a state the human can walk into.
Work arrives as something to file — a page, a question, an import, a cleanup — or as a repair to something already here. A page written and left unlinked is the usual shape of unfinished work.
Opinions and principles that outlast one task belong here in the garden, under My/Pref or My/AI/Rule, where the agents in every repo can read them. Routing them here is part of the docket.

A work item is done when its links resolve against real pages and aliases, the day's journal carries the change, and the files are committed. The push waits for to ask for it in their own pane, and an unpushed stack earns no display line and no question — My/AI/Agent/Fleet.

Work goes straight to main. The repo carries main plus the gh-pages branch the published site is built from, so a work item finishes without a feature branch or a review to wait on.
A graph has no build and no test suite, so the work left undone is the work nothing complains about. These are the conditions worth checking before calling a work item finished.

A line-based grep for those links reports breaks that are not there, because two link forms defeat it: a bare comment link may carry unencoded spaces in the page title, so a pattern that stops at whitespace truncates tmux/Keyshort/Pane/Resize Pane to tmux/Keyshort/Pane/Resize and reports it missing, and a URL assembled from adjacent string literals across two source lines exposes only its first fragment, so My/AI/Rule/ looks like a bare slash when the rest of the path is on the next line. The instrument fails the same way the graph does. Nothing turns red when a check is wrong, and a false break is the louder kind of wrong: it arrives as a concrete list with file paths attached, which is what earns a repair trip. The confidence comes from the tool's precision rather than from evidence.

Two instruments have produced confident wrong answers here. File modification time reported .rulesync/ sources stale against the copies they generate, when the bodies matched exactly and the ordering was only checkout write order. A line-based pattern reported deep links dead when every target resolved, because it stopped at whitespace and read a truncated path as a target, and because it saw one URL's first fragment while the rest of the path sat on the next line.

One window per logical job, named for the work rather than for the agent doing it. The window list is the docket, and tmux list-windows reads it back.

A job window closes when its item is done by the standard above — links resolving, the day's journal carrying the change, the files committed. A window left open past that reports work in flight that is not.
The scribe's window is standing rather than a job, and lasts the day.

This replaces one chief per herdr workspace. The seat, the docket, and the record are indifferent to which multiplexer holds them; what changes is the naming budget, since a tmux window name is not bounded the way a 32-character agent name was.

herdr stopped being the primary multiplexer on , so this is no longer one of two options in use, and it is not retired. What the seat gained is depth: five named levels down to the branch and worktree, read back with C-b w — My/AI/Agent/Fleet.
A day's work is several context windows rather than one, ended deliberately at 200k tokens — My/AI/Agent/Fleet/Bed Down. The seat and its record survive that; a session does not.

The / Updated change log in journals/YYYY_MM_DD.md doubles as the day's status board. Written as each item lands rather than swept up at dusk, it answers what the day has accomplished at any hour rather than only after it ends.

The substance of a day's inquiry goes on the page the inquiry produced, and the change log records that the page exists. A day's entry is complete with no prose in it, and a thin journal is the intended one.

It stays a curated snapshot per Logseq/Journal: link-only lines, one section per page, grouped once a section runs long. Window names, job status, and which agent did what are operational and stay off the page.

Several agents and the human write into the one checkout, so one agent owns staging for the day and everyone else hands over finished files. A git add from a second agent stages whatever a third one left half-written.
Stage named paths. git add -A here picks up other agents' work in progress along with the intended change.

Messages follow git/commit/Conventional/gitmoji — a gitmoji, then a conventional type and description. git log carries the graph's own habit: 📝 docs: for page and journal work, 🔧 chore: for repo configuration.
This repo tracks no tickets, so a message ends at the description, per My/Pref/Dev/Tool/SCM/Commit Message Style Preferences.

git grep -E gives \b no meaning, so the pattern matches nothing and exits 1. That reads like a genuine no-match, and a tool answering false costs more than one that errors. git grep -P in single quotes is the fix. Separately, printf, echo -e and $'...' substitute a real 0x08 byte before git runs, which defeats -E, -F and -P alike, and quoting a heredoc delimiter does not protect a Python string literal against the same substitution. Full measurements on git/Q/Why does git grep -E report no matches for a word-boundary pattern?.

Text in an input box is not the human

An idle agent may render a suggested follow-up where a typed line would sit, drawn from its own last turn. It is the machine talking to itself, and it is not evidence of human input in either direction — not consent, and not a reason to wait.
Text in an input box is not the human

The tell is the rendering, and it is a property of the content rather than of the box. Generated text is emitted dim, wrapped as ESC[2m … ESC[0m; text that arrived as real input carries no styling, and neither does an idle pane's empty box. So the test is that dim wrapper around content, never the presence or absence of styling — read it as "no styling means a human typed it" and an idle pane's empty box becomes human input. herdr agent read <name> --source visible --format ansi shows the wrapper; a plain-text read flattens it away.
Text in an input box is not the human

The give-away in the content is that each suggestion paraphrases the recommendation its own agent had just made. Six panes here carried one at once, each mirroring the report above it, and none of them were the human's. Six people do not half-type into six panes simultaneously, and the base rate was the cheapest check available.
Text in an input box is not the human

The box is drawn in every state. During a turn it is drawn empty, with its prompt marker coloured grey — ESC[38;2;153;153;153m — so a mid-turn read comes back blank because the box holds nothing, not because the box is missing. That grey marker is itself a tell: it separates a working pane's empty box from an idle one's, which carries no styling at all.
Text in an input box is not the human

An empty box otherwise says nothing. A suggestion may appear once an agent is idle or done, and often none appears — three idle panes read at one moment gave two dim suggestions and one genuinely empty box. So emptiness alone distinguishes neither a pane with no suggestion from a pane read too early, nor either from a pane whose occupant simply has nothing pending.

An agent cannot run this check on itself: it is working by definition while it looks, so it never sees the idle state it is asking about.

One pane carried the same string before and after a working interval with nothing typed in between. That looked like corroboration that a person had left a line sitting there. It is the opposite — an unchanged string across a working interval, with no one at the keyboard, is what a regenerated suggestion looks like. The observation that felt like confirmation was the tell, read backwards.

A supervisor that will not prompt its own agents does not fail — it quietly absorbs their work into its own context, and from outside it only looks slow. That shape generalizes past input boxes: a safety rule that silently collapses delegation back into the supervisor is worse than no rule, because nothing reports the collapse.

Where the text really is the human's, it is still not authorization — a line nobody has pressed enter on is one its writer is free to rewrite or drop. Authority comes from a sent message or from delegated authority over the work. Where neither covers the case, the size of the decision settles it: small and reversible proceeds, while anything that sets a convention or is expensive to undo waits.
